Lecture 10 The Hypergeometric Distribution, the Poisson Distribution, Poisson Processes and the Poisson Approximation to the Binomial

Counting successes when drawing without replacement (the hypergeometric distribution), the Poisson distribution and the Poisson process that produces it, a call-center example, and a proof that binomial probabilities tend to Poisson probabilities when n is large and np stays fixed.

1The hypergeometric distribution

Hypergeometric Distributions

Suppose objects in a population of objects have a certain property and the remaining objects do not.

If objects are selected without replacement and all remaining objects are equally likely to be selected at each step of the selection process, what is the probability you select objects with this property?

Definition

If counts the number of objects selected with the property, then is a hypergeometric random variable.

(left blank on this photo; the formula is filled in on the next one)

✎ Explanation (added)

This is the situation from the end of Lecture 9: sampling without replacement. It is not binomial, because the draws are not independent. With the urn below, the chance the first ball is white is , but if the first one was white, the chance the second is white drops to . The hypergeometric distribution is the exact answer in that case; the binomial with is only an approximation, and Lecture 9's 5% rule says when that approximation is good enough.

Three numbers describe the situation: the population size , how many in it have the property, , and the sample size . The phrase "all remaining objects are equally likely at each step" is what makes every set of objects equally likely, so classical probability (Lecture 4) can be used.

4Poisson processes

Poisson distributions are useful when dealing with Poisson processes.

Poisson Processes

Suppose we are counting the number of occurrences of some event in a given time interval (or length wire or …) and that it is reasonable to assume the following are valid.

Assumptions
  1. ① In a short time interval of length , the probability of an event occurring is directly proportional to the length of the time interval so it is equal to for some constant .
    The probability that more than one event occurs is 0 so the probability that no event occurs in this time interval is .
  2. ② The probability of an event occurring in a time interval only "depends on the length" of the time interval and not where it is located.
  3. ③ If two intervals are disjoint, then the knowledge that a certain number of events have occurred in one time interval has no effect on the probability that any number of events have occurred in the other time interval.
✎ Explanation (added)

In plain words. ① Events come one at a time, and in a very short window the chance of one is proportional to the window's length; is the rate (events per unit time). ② The rate doesn't change over time: a 5-minute window at 9:00 behaves like a 5-minute window at 3:00. ③ Events in non-overlapping windows are independent: a busy minute tells you nothing about the next minute.

"(or length wire or …)": the "interval" doesn't have to be time. Flaws along a length of wire, or typos over pages, work the same way when the same three assumptions hold.

③ If two intervals are disjoint, … (as above)

If counts the number of occurrences of the event in a time interval of length , then

(Relatively easy to find justifications online. The binomial approach is one of the easier ones.)

✎ Explanation (added)

The binomial approach. Cut into short pieces of length . By ① each piece holds 0 or 1 events, with . By ② every piece has the same probability, and by ③ the pieces are independent. So the number of events is a binomial count, , with no matter how fine the cut. Letting gives exactly the Poisson pmf with . That limit is the one proved at the end of this lecture (section 6), so the last part of the lecture is also the justification for this formula.

Textbook Devore §3.6, p. 134, "The Poisson Process": three assumptions and the Proposition . The book's assumption 1 says one event has probability , and its assumption 2 says more than one has probability (negligible compared with ) where the board says 0. The board's ② (only the length matters) is not listed separately in the book; it is built into the constant rate . The book's assumption 3 is the board's ③. p. 135 extends the idea to counts in an area or volume.

  • Examples 3.35–3.36 (pp. 127–128). Capture–recapture: 5 tagged animals among 25, a second sample of 10. Works , , then the mean and variance (variance 1, against 1.6 with replacement) and how the same idea estimates an unknown .
  • Example 3.38 (p. 132). Defects in a transistor with : one probability from the pmf and a cumulative one read from Appendix Table A.2.
  • Example 3.39 (p. 133). Pages with typos in a 600-page novel: the binomial and its Poisson approximation side by side, with Table 3.2 showing how the fit improves as grows.
  • Example 3.41 (pp. 134–135). Pulses arriving at 6 per minute; for a half-minute window , and "at least one" by the complement.

What a typical exam question looks like
  • A population with two kinds of objects, a sample drawn without replacement: name the distribution and its parameters (, , ), then find , , and , , like the urn example.
  • Decide between hypergeometric and binomial for the same situation (with or without replacement, the 5% rule), and compare the two variances.
  • A count with a given mean: , "at most", "at least", "more than" by the complement, or "within one standard deviation of the mean" using .
  • A rate per hour or minute and a different interval: find first, then the probability, as in the call-center example.
  • A binomial with large and small : check , , approximate with Poisson, and possibly compare with the exact binomial value.
  • Show (or ) for a Poisson variable from the definition; your typed note flags this as a possible exam question.
